title: India's Supreme Court Just Killed the Online Gaming Industry. The Tax Bill Is ₹2.5 Lakh Crore.
excerpt: The court upheld 28% GST on all bets — retroactively. Lawyers say mass insolvencies are now inevitable for the once-thriving startup sector.
body:
India's Supreme Court on May 27 upheld a 28% goods and services tax on all real-money online gaming — and ruled that the levy applies retroactively, validating over ₹1.5 trillion in tax demands that gaming companies say they cannot pay.

The verdict, delivered by a bench of Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Justice R. Mahadevan, dismissed more than 100 petitions filed by online gaming companies, casinos, turf clubs, and industry bodies. The court's central finding: online gaming platforms are not mere intermediaries facilitating skill-based games. They are suppliers of "actionable claims" — a legal term for betting and gambling — and are taxable on the full face value of every bet, not just on platform fees.

## The Numbers Are Staggering

The Directorate General of GST Intelligence had issued show-cause notices totaling over ₹1.5 trillion to gaming companies between 2022 and 2023. A single notice to Gameskraft Technologies was worth ₹21,000 crore. With the Supreme Court's ruling, the total estimated liability across the sector now stands at approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore.

"It is impossible for the companies to pay the tax liabilities that have been proposed by the GST authorities," said Jay Sayta, a technology and gaming lawyer. "While a copy of the judgment is awaited, companies will explore the option of approaching the GST Council for relief on the retrospective tax dues."

Sudipta Bhattacharjee, partner at Khaitan & Co who represented several gaming companies, was blunter: "In many cases, the online money gaming companies may themselves be forced to voluntarily declare insolvency. In other cases, the GST department, as operational creditors, may also end up moving NCLT for declaring online money gaming companies as insolvent."

## How It Got Here

The dispute began in 2022 when the DGGI alleged that gaming firms had been underpaying GST by taxing only their commissions and platform fees, rather than the entire value of deposits and bets placed by users. Gaming companies argued they merely facilitated skill-based games and that prize pools belonged to users, not platforms.

The GST Council responded in August 2023 by amending the law to impose a uniform 28% GST on the "full face value" of all bets, deposits, and entry amounts — effective October 1, 2023. The industry insisted this was a new levy that could not be applied retroactively. The government countered that the amendment merely clarified existing law.

The Supreme Court sided with the government. The 2023 amendment was "clarificatory, not retrospective," the bench held, meaning the 28% rate was always the correct interpretation.

## The Diaspora Investment Angle

For Indian Americans who invested in India's once-booming online gaming sector, the ruling is devastating. Several gaming startups — including Dream11, which was valued at over $8 billion at its peak — attracted significant investment from NRI and foreign venture capital. Dream11 declined to comment on the verdict.

"What sets an unexpected precedent is that private investors of once-unicorn startups will now have to write off big-ticket investments," said a senior lawyer representing multiple gaming firms.

The irony is hard to miss. In August 2025, Parliament enacted the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, banning real-money games involving monetary stakes. Most ventures had already shut down or pivoted. Now the court has slapped a massive tax bill on companies that largely no longer have revenue.

## What Comes Next

The industry's options are limited. Legal experts say challenges could include appealing to a larger Supreme Court bench or negotiating directly with the GST Council. But individual GST notices will still undergo adjudication, which could give companies some room to contest the quantum of demands, penalties, and calculation methodology.

One lawyer raised an unexpected constitutional wrinkle: by treating online gaming as betting and gambling — a state subject under India's constitution — the Supreme Court may have inadvertently undermined the Centre's own ban on the sector. If gaming is gambling, it falls under state jurisdiction, not central law.

For now, the sector that once employed thousands and attracted billions in investment is facing a terminal tax bill it cannot pay, for an activity it is no longer permitted to conduct.
